description.narrative: Just Future’s vision is of a world in which all people in fragile states benefit from more accessible, responsive and accountable security and justice institutions, and more inclusive arrangements for political governance and peace-making.

The Just Future (JF) programme is a 5 years programme funded under the ‘Power of Voices’ framework by the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Cordaid leads the Just Future Alliance that joins 6 coalition partners, 3 research institutions, around 25 local CSOs and an international civil society network. Through this partnership we work to strengthen capacity of civil society organizations in their role of lobby and advocacy. This will build on the previous phase of the strategic partnership from the MOFA called : “Dialogue and Dissent”- 2016-2020.
Fragility, conflict and violence are the most significant obstacles to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Just 20% of fragile and conflict-affected states are on track to achieve SDG targets by 2030, when 85% of the world’s poorest people will be concentrated in those states; millions of people living in fragile contexts are at risk of being left behind. As it addresses fragility directly, SDG16 on peaceful, just, and inclusive societies is a vital accelerator of Agenda 2030. In the most fragile and conflict-affected contexts, insecurity and injustice is chronic and widespread due to weak, unresponsive institutions that do not meet the needs and claims of security and justice seekers, with adverse impact on the dignity, prosperity, and survival of all in society. The prevalence of insecurity and injustice also undermines people’s perception of the efficacy and legitimacy of the state, inducing the weak social contract at the heart of fragility. In 6 countries—Afghanistan, Burundi, Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Mali, Niger and South Sudan—fragility also manifests as lack of freedom and space for independent civic action. All 6 countries are amongst the world’s least free and most closed, due to repressive legislation and regulation by states, conservative or patriarchal social norms and informal institutions that restrict space for women and youth, the actions of violent non-state actors, or a combination thereof. In the cases of Afghanistan, Mali, and South Sudan, deficient processes of peacemaking or peace implementation are also present; 5 countries (all but Burundi) host large international peace and security assistance missions. Civil society organizations (CSOs), community-based organizations (CBOs), social movements, and informal activist groups in all 6 countries are working to improve security and justice and make political decision-making and peace processes more inclusive. CSOs, CBOs, social movements, and informal activist groups can aggregate and articulate the needs and demands of the most excluded constituencies, and engage on their behalf with duty-bearers and power-holders. But the relative weakness, fragmentation, and contested legitimacy of civil society in a context of shrinking civic space undermines the capacity of these actors to advocate for effective institutions or negotiate and collaborate with the state. Consequently, the demands and expectations of the most excluded are seldom reflected in the policy and practices of security, justice, governance and peace actors at the sub-national and national levels.
The project will work with CSOs, CBOs, social movements, informal activist groups and community members (women and youth) as the primary stakeholders.

Each of the four priority themes raised by the coalition appeared in the interventions of various Member States. The final outcome reflected a strong alignment with the civil-society agenda: of the 284 recommendations issued to the DRC, 235 were accepted by the government, including several directly linked to civic space, protection of HRDs, IDPs, youth and women’s participation, and transitional justice. During the Knowledge Platform Security & Rule of Law Annual Conference (KPAC24) in Dakar, Cordaid and its partner, RENEDEPP, organized a high-visibility side event focused on Customary and Informal Justice (CIJ) in Mali, highlighting its importance for access to justice. Eight young men and women from Mali and Niger who attended the Youth Summit met with officials from ECOWAS and UNOWAS and presented a five-point advocacy document urging the two regional bodies to include the youth in all their mediation efforts and other dealings with the military junta. The Just Future and EurAc delegation secured bilateral meetings, including with France and Sierra Leone (penholder and co-penholder) and the DRC delegation for advocacy on the Monusco mandate. Cordaid, in partnership with WIPC, acted as a catalyst by mobilizing resources, coordinating data collection, and preparing the UPR shadow report, while also facilitating advocacy efforts in Geneva within a broader coalition which had an impact on key stakeholders. The Peace Centre led the process of developing a Policy for a minimum of 30% gender quota for women’s participation in all conflict prevention and management, missions, peace processes, and election observation missions led by the African Union. WANEP in collaboration with Just Future alliance members in Niger and Mali, selected youth from the two countries, prepared them and organised the advocacy meeting between the youth and the ECOWAS and UNOWAS officials in Accra. On the occasion of the HR Ambassador of the NL to Burundi, Cordaid met with the ambassador priori to the visit and shared an advocacy note with recommendations. Cordaid participated in the WHRD toolkit review. WIPC facilitated the WHRDs from South Sudan during an online FGD. Since 2019 CSPPS prepares (together with the TAP network) an annual Civil Society Declaration on SDG16+, which is officially launched and presented during the Conference. CSPPS spearheads the Voices of SDG16+ Campaign each year with partners from the Global SDG16 Coalition. CSPPS assesses the videos (with partners) and organises and hosts the event online. The Expert Group Meeting on SDG16 in New York has invited CSPPs to become a member. The Peace Centre led the process of developing a Policy for a minimum of 30% gender quota for women’s participation in all conflict prevention and management, missions, peace processes, and election observation missions led by the African Union. WANEP initiated the Youth Summit that took place in Accra in June 2024. WANEP supported youth in Mali and Niger who managed to initiate the process of developing National Action Plans (NAPs) on UNSCR 2250 on Youth, Peace and Security. The Coalition strategically used the UPR Pre-sessions as a high-level advocacy platform to bring urgent concerns directly to UN Member States and the DRC government."

"The dissemination of SIPRI's research's findings on the UNMISS mandate renewal was instrumental for global advocacy. We were able to involve Just Future Partners from South Sudan and, together, we delivered recommendations on the role of civil society in the transition, the inclusion of women and youth. Presentations by to the MINUSMA Integrated Operations Team (IOT) in NYC and our co-organized event with the Dutch mission, have led to impactful research dissemination and engagement. These efforts generated substantial interest and recognition, highlighting the value of our findings. KUNO report (https://www.kuno-platform.nl/themes/learning-from-20-years-of-dutch-involvement-in-afghanistan/) finalized and handed to Dutch MFA, Dutch MoD, IOB and Parliament. By highlighting several key aspects of a people-centred approach to DDR, the Council Conclusions provide strong political backing that helps to cement this as the EU’s approach when it comes to supporting DDR in JFA countries and beyond. This meeting was to influence ECOWAS to ensure the theme for the Ambassadors thematic meeting is based on inclusivity. The mission of the Kingdom of the Netherlands to the UN Security Council prioritized women's political participation as one of the top 3 priorities in their speech during the open debate at the UN Security Council on WPS. title.narrative: Number of International agreements influenced by primary stakeholders (CSOs) that lead to more effective, accountable, inclusive, transparent and responsive security institutions

description.narrative: A robust legal framework, which is translated in inclusive policies, is essential to regulate well-functioning Security and Justice Institutions, and Peace Processes (3 Outcome Areas). Through L&A the JFA aims to influence policy reform. With this indicator, we aim to measure the number of laws and policies influenced result in changes benefitting our constituencies.

comment.narrative: EU Council Conclusions on DDR support “people-centred”, & “conflict-sensitive” DDR, highlight links to peacebuilding, and include much strengthened language on YPS. We expect that this will lead to more concrete results.

"EEAS staff has drafted a communication text together with SFCG as input for political negotiations on the EU DRR strategic approach. While this has not yet been translated into international agreements, we expect that this will lead to more concrete results in 2022. First of a series of workshops in each of the four countries in which ASSN is active, held in December, to create inclusive and cross-cutting, 'bottom-up' dialogue with security sector officials around the AU SSR Policy Framework. Cordaid partner Crisis Action Sahel had some key successes. There has been considerable affirmation of CA/People Sahel Coalition recommendations by key policymakers. AU Commissioner for Political Affairs, Peace and Security, Ambassador Bankole Adeoye, told CA that the AU “needs to adopt your new focus on a people-centred approach”. France’s Sahel Envoy described the CA/Sahel poeple Coalition report as “an approach that France agrees and adheres to”. And UN Security Council members such as the UK and Norway are declaring that their Sahel strategies now “align...with the People’s Coalition”. "

"New EU Civilian Compact now includes commitments on better human rights due diligence, systematically applying conflict sensitivity and the do-no-harm, more regular and inclusive cooperation and dialogue with civil society, impact-oriented evaluation, targeting mandates to local needs, mainstreaming gender, and promoting Youth, Peace and Security European Parliament’s resolution on implementation of civilian CSDP and other EU civilian security assistance (with a view to the Civilian Compact update) includes key language on impact-oriented evaluation, local needs, civil society engagement, conflict sensitivity, security sector governance and accountability, relations between security forces and civilians, and YPS. Influencing political declaration for SDG Summit - actors influenced include UN member states and wider SDG16 community. The UN SSRUnit commissioned ASSN to produce a Policy Note on Hybrid Security and Security Governance in Africa ASSN was the technical partner to the African Union in the drafting of the Policy Framework on people-centred security."

"The AU has signalled its commitment by adopting the Operational Guidance Note (OGN) on Security Sector Oversight and Accountability during the year, the drafting of which was led by ASSN’s regional node for Southern Africa, the African Police Civilian Oversight Forum (APCOF).

"Two UN institutions, the UN SSRUnit and the UN SSR Expert Roster of which ASSN is member, have used input from ASSN in the development of two increasingly prominent emerging SSR approaches : ""hybridity security"" and ""people-centred security"". December 2024 UNSC resolution on MONUSCO incorporates critical aspects taken from the recommendations prepared by JFA with key stakeholders."
